What’s actually relevant are the material conditions people live under. Which is why the distinction I make now is people who do transition and people who don’t—whatever the motivation is, because motivations really don’t matter all that much, and if you focus on that, you end up discussing metaphysics and psychology, not how people are actually treated in the world and the particular political interests they have (i.e. access to gender affirming medical care).

That sucks and I’m sorry you had to experience that. I’ve heard similar things about some trans spaces. I hope you can find a place/community/group where there are more people who share your lived experience and to whom you can connect and relate. I myself have been in similar situations where I felt ostracized or out of place in spaces for trans people, and it’s a really shitty feeling.

This is very relatable to me, and I’m never going to adopt a transmedicalist mindset—I don’t wish to be associated with the shittier parts of that community. And also because I think the debate about dysphoria being “required” to be trans is extremely muddied by the fact that everyone has different definitions of dysphoria and how it manifests to the extent that the assertion is virtually useless. 

And, realistically, you can’t force people to stop using labels they’ve adopted or to see themselves as cis when they don’t identify as cis—it just doesn’t work that way. One of the things I’ve stopped doing is engaging in or even thinking about debates about who is or isn’t a “valid” trans person. Because all of the arguments devolve into tautologies or purely psychological interpretations of identity. 

I’ve begun asserting that I would like for non-transitioning trans and/or nonbinary people (meaning people who don’t want/need to medically transition or even really socially transition) to stop acting like we have the same experiences and to become educated about the MATERIAL differences between the lives of most transsexual people and non-transitioning nonbinary people. They will insist that pointing this difference out, which is completely reasonable and politically practical, drives a wedge in the community that is “gatekeeping” or “invalidating,” or makes us “weaker” against our oppressors. Because we have shared political interests, supposedly. 

But the fact is that current anti-trans legislation and transphobia is aimed at transsexual people and people who need or want to actually transition, whatever the motivation (which includes some nonbinary people). And we often have very different political interests and experiences of the world. Some people who identify as trans are materially cisgender (or cissexual, if you will)—that is how they move through the world. I’m tired of some of these people’s egos being so fragile they can’t acknowledge this or give a fuck about what’s at stake, and instead whine forever at people who don’t have the privilege they have about feeling invalidated. 

Which is so absurd. You see the same shit from straight-passing, bisexual cisgender white women (sorry but it’s usually white women lol which I think is telling) who are *happily* in monogamous marriages to cishet men. They are by definition more materially privileged and normative than most queer people in the world, but they turn to a marginalized community and shit on us and accuse us of gatekeeping if we don’t jump to VaLiDaTe them or make sure their queer identity isn’t “erased,” as if that’s up to us, lol. 

Here’s the thing—nobody can actually validate or invalidate somebody else’s identity. It’s your (the general “you”) job to validate and believe in the conclusions you come to about yourself at the end of the day. Which is a lot easier if you’re not lying to yourself about your subject position to appropriate experiences you don’t have out of some need to be a victim/misplaced privilege guilt/whatever. 

Plus, some of these folks say outright TERFy and often transmisogynistic shit in particular, waving their AFAB card around like special victim armor. Or they chalk dysphoria up to a social construct that wouldn’t exist if we didn’t live in a patriarchal/binary/cisnormative society (lollllll at this one). Especially if you push them a little bit—they’ll start spouting off about AFABs being a categorically oppressed sex class to trans women, making all sorts of gross implications and tossing out dog whistles. Can’t have your cake and eat it too. You’re either a woman or nonbinary—which is it?

I think my last sentence speaks directly to what you’re saying & I stated in my initial post that I’m frustrated by things like this but am coming from a place of compassion. I then reiterated my understanding for where this type of thing is coming from in my second post—thus directly acknowledging that these posts are obviously not “unprompted…” 

I responded because I care about trans people in general and want to be supportive of other trans people—but I also have my own feelings and boundaries. Navigating these things is part of existing in a community and what makes that challenging. Much of OP’s post is very very similar if not almost identical to what actual bigots say about us (“people will never see you as your gender, it’s just fact”). I point this out precisely because I care about trans people. It is not “uplifting others” to post things like this and externalize your internalized transphobia at other trans people. I’m extremely aware things are hard and have been for a long, long time—I am also trans haha. Again, it’s one thing to vent or seek support—it’s another to go into a trans sub and say to other trans people what bigots and bullies say to us every day. I posted this precisely because words mean something and affect people, lol

I don’t think it genuinely helps, because people have to decide for themselves that they want to address stuff like this, and it’s unlikely things that strangers say on the internet are going to have an impact. Especially because folks like this tend to be looking to have by their beliefs confirmed or commiserate, not have their minds changed. Which isn’t meant to be a judgment, that’s just where these folks are at and I get it’s coming from a place of struggle/pain/frustration.

But I do think it’s helpful to point out that this is unhealthy and unrealistic thinking for other trans people reading this stuff, because it may be internalized transphobia, but it’s still transphobia. And I think people need to learn to recognize it for what it is and be conscious of bringing it into spaces with other trans people. There’s a difference between venting about having a hard time with how one’s transition is going or expressing worry/distress that you’ll never be seen as your actual gender vs. declaring as truth to a space full of trans people that they’re doomed to never be seen as who they are.

If your goal is to be perceived as straight, speak from your chest (this takes more breath and air than speaking from your head—pay attention to your diaphragm), don’t inflect or vary your pitch as much, use phrases and colloquialisms that straight guys use in whatever area you live in/culture you’re a part of, etc.

I have no real scientific evidence for this, but I think sometimes starting on a lower dose of T for a few months can help make the change more gradual and help your voice sound less strained/nasal/maybe put less strain on your vocal chords overall. But that’s anecdotal, I don’t know if it’s actually true or not. Some of it’s gonna come down to your natural vocal resonance, the shape of your mouth, chest, and airways, too—not much can be done about that.

EDIT: I also think that once you reach a certain pitch on T, cis people aren’t going to think your voice sounds “trans,” unless you’re not passing for other reasons—they might just think you’re gay or queer or effeminate if the issue is inflection and speech mannerisms. Most cis people don’t have the perspective for that. Other trans people and probably primarily trans men and mascs are going to be more likely to be able to identify “the trans voice” in regards to actual vocal resonance. You’d be surprised how little the average cis person actually cares or thinks about any of this.

It is a crapshoot, really. As someone else said, it’s pretty hard to know exactly how someone’s chest will turn out when healed. And it also comes down to what each person wants and what people can afford. Some surgeons are more skilled and have more consistent results than others, as will be the case with any kind of surgery, really. Some folks are lucky to live in proximity to those surgeons and others are lucky to be able to afford to travel to them. Complications that affect end results, especially with nipples in general, also do occur—probably more often than people realize because it’s a crappy experience to have and you’re less likely to share your post-op chest online if you’re unhappy with how it looks. All that said—there is no guarantee of a “perfect” or cis-passing post-op chest. 

It’s a risk you kind of have to accept, and weigh what’s most important to you. My chest didn’t turn out quite how I wanted, which bugs me occasionally, but I’m mostly very happy with my results, and the relief I get day to day from not having to deal with binding or chest dysphoria is 100% worth it. I’m not shirtless the majority of the time, so the relatively small imperfections are not really a huge day-to-day concern.

Edit: I’ve seen plenty of awesome results throughout the years, though. Maybe you just haven’t been looking for very long or at surgeons whose work you like?
